newsitem.title: USA: Congress, White House forge ahead in budget talks.
newsitem.headline: Congress, White House forge ahead in budget talks.

text.p: Republicans greeted President Clinton's requests to spend more for education and health with "thunderous silence" Friday, but the two sides agreed to give balanced budget talks one more week.
House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich, Republican of Ohio, said the two sides were still "worlds apart" in their views of the role of government and its need to spend money.
The Republican plan, as Kasich described it, would free local governments to take action rather than allocate federal dollars for the projects as the administration has requested.
"It may be that we are just simply too far apart, we don't know yet," Kasich said.

The chief Democrat on the Senate Budget Committee, Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, asked whether the Republicans nodded assent on any of Clinton's requests, told reporters: "The thunderous silence with which they greeted it indicated some degree of their views."
Four lengthy budget negotiations were held this week covering taxes, Medicare health care for the elderly, education, and other government spending.
Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici said the push for an agreement will continue with a series of meetings next week. Monday's will focus on Medicaid for the poor.
Domenici said he took heart that both the administration and Republicans showed willingness to move toward agreement.

"Without agreeing on things it's pretty obvious that the administration is willing to give in some areas that are important to us and we have indicated a willingness on our part to give in some areas that are important to them," the New Mexico Republican said.

Congressional aides said next week's talks would likely determine whether the talks could move to the next stage, serious bargaining on programmes and spending, or whether the Republicans would work to develop a budget with only conservative Democrats.

The top White House budget negotiator, Office of Management and Budget Director Franklin Raines, told reporters no decisions were made in the meeting with House and Senate Budget Committee leaders of both parties.
"I think there were expressions of agreement with a number of things that we said and expressions of disagreement with a number of things," Raines said.

"We are determined to keep working to see if such a negotiation can yield an agreement. The jury is out," he added, emphasising that the president does want to reach a budget agreement that can be supported by both parties.

The discussions centred on the president's effort to provide tax credits and deductions for higher education as well as expand available health care for children. Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala presented the health initiatives offered by the president.

Clinton's budget proposal would make education a top priority and increase spending for this area to $46.4 billion, nearly $9 billion more than the Republican-controlled Congress approved last year. It would also add $3.1 billion for the environment and $1.1 billion to fight crime.
His tax proposal includes deductions for higher educaton worth $36.1 billion over five years.
Not yet on the table are Republican requests for higher defence spending and the various Republican tax cut proposals, which would nearly double the president's tax cut offer.
